content.p: In November 1988 about 550 police officers, some in uniform and some in plain clothes, searched 38 homes, four clubhouses, three pubs and seven brothels and arrested 13 men, all of them members of a motorcycle club called Gremium. That evening the head of the Baden-Württemberg state criminal police office presented a weapons collection on television, along with a long list of grave allegations. The state interior ministry in Stuttgart banned the club that day as a "criminal association". According to the weekly Der Spiegel, in its issue of 8 April 1990, the main trial had just ended with the club's president, Michael Heyer, acquitted, and with even the prosecutor no longer mentioning the central accusation, that the club itself was a criminal association, in his closing speech.

That collapse did not end official suspicion of the club. German intelligence and police reports have continued to name Gremium alongside the Hells Angels, the Bandidos and the Outlaws, and in 2013 the federal interior minister broke up one of its regional associations. The club, for its part, presents itself as a traditional motorcycle club that obeys German law and says that politicians and the press paint it as criminal without justification. This account follows both versions, with each claim credited to whoever made it. Quotations from German and Danish sources are translated here.
content.h2: A student's moped club that grew
content.p: Gremium dates itself to 1972 in Mannheim. Der Spiegel reported in 1990 that Michael Heyer, by then a former law student, had started it that year as a 17-year-old moped rider; by 1990 he ran a travel agency and an automotive-accessories business. The club's own history page says it staged the "Presi-Rally", a meeting of German motorcycle clubs, on the Friesenheimer Insel in Mannheim in 1978 together with the Bones MC, and hosted it alone in 1983, 1986 and 1995. In 1986, it says, it was a founding member of the Biker Union, a body representing German bikers.

The club's symbols are part of its story. The club's back patch, or colour, shows, in its words, a rising sun and a clenched fist stretching into the sky, which it says express its attitude and strength. The club's history page explains a numerical wordplay: G is the seventh letter of the alphabet, and the name Gremium has seven letters. B.T. and Ekstra Bladet trace the name "Black Seven", used by support groups and by a Danish splinter group, to the same wordplay. On 1 July 2004, after 32 years, the club changed its colour. The old Celtic cross gave way, by majority vote according to the club, to the Iron Cross, and the names of individual German cities were replaced across the board by the single word "Germany". The club says many members welcomed the change because the Celtic cross was often mistaken for the Christian cross, and it adds that it has never restricted its members' political views or religion. It also says it distances itself from both "right" and "left" ideas.

By the club's account, new members do not simply join: they serve a long probation period in which they get to know everyone and become known themselves. In its own 2012 description it listed numerous chapters in Germany and more in Italy, Poland, the Canary Islands, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Austria and Thailand.

Der Spiegel's reconstruction of the raid opens with Heyer himself: he did not know where the men came from, and then saw pistol barrels pointed at him as 15 officers surrounded him and one handcuffed him. The magazine said the 13 arrests were of club members. On television that evening, the president of the Baden-Württemberg criminal police office, Ralf Krüger, presented a large weapons collection and a long list of grave allegations: drug dealing, protection extortion, aggravated assault and breach of the peace. The interior ministry banned the club the same day.

Banning a club as a whole depends on the federal associations law. A published headnote from a Baden-Württemberg administrative court case on the ban of a nationwide motorcycle club (1 S 3626/88) sets out the legal test. A nationwide club formed by the merger of clubs from different cities, with a common name and a uniform emblem, counts as an association under the federal associations law, and that status does not depend on whether its local groups qualify as sub-organisations. The criminal conduct of individual members can be attributed to such an association with local chapters if it shapes the character of the whole association at the time of the ban order. The headnote as saved does not name the club.

The criminal trial that followed was heavy machinery. Der Spiegel counted two newly created chambers at the regional court in Karlsruhe, six judges, 20 defendants, more than 20 lawyers and nearly 100 witnesses over three months. Writing in the issue of 8 April 1990, after the verdicts the previous week, the magazine judged that the show of force had come to little. The presiding judge, Eva-Marie Wollentin, said the effort had been grossly excessive and had been needed only because investigators had apparently not weighed exculpatory material and had relied on mere assumptions. Heyer's lawyer, Gerhard Härdle, called the investigators' approach "organised sloppiness".

The magazine listed what some of the supposed evidence had turned out to be. According to Der Spiegel, the "cocaine" was dental powder used for bite impressions, a carbine was a decoration, and a pimps' price list was an ordinary brothel sheet. Police speculation about turnover in the millions was contradicted by the club's two accounts, which held 4,872.57 and 15.37 marks; the court told the investigators that they had simply added up several years of private income. A witness was sent home after he turned out to be an assistant of the criminal police, and the police had recruited several club members who were willing to talk as informants.

The court did convict. Sixteen of the club's roughly 300 members were convicted of assault, weapons possession, pimping and drug offences. But the court found, as Der Spiegel reported, that they had committed those offences privately and that the motorcycle club had nothing to do with them. The state police chief, Alfred Stümper, took a different view of the outcome. He called it normal: a huge investigation with many overtime hours, and "a little mouse comes out" at the end.

The club remained banned when the article went to print, and about 180,000 marks of Heyer's assets, which the authorities treated as alleged club property, remained seized; he was suing over that. Baden-Württemberg's interior minister, Dietmar Schlee, said the state would hold on to the ban. Der Spiegel put the cost to taxpayers of the Karlsruhe trial alone at several hundred thousand marks, not counting detention compensation in five figures. The club's version, on its own history page, is that apart from a few members kept in custody on drug possession and other "not especially serious cases", most of those arrested were soon released, that the ban was lifted three years later, and that the proceedings cost millions that the state paid. In its 2017 statement the club adds that the Baden-Württemberg administrative court found in 1992 that it was not a "criminal-structured" organisation. That claim is the club's own, and the pages opened for this account do not show the court's judgment. B.T. wrote in 2014 that the ban was lifted again in 1992 because it had not been possible to prove that Gremium was a criminal organisation.

After the ban, Gremium kept appearing in security-service assessments, usually next to the larger rival clubs. The Bavarian domestic-intelligence report for 2005 grouped motorcycle gangs under organised crime. It said that behaviour typical of organised crime, including drug offences, human trafficking, assaults and protection extortion, committed with a division of labour, had repeatedly been found among members of the best-known groups, naming the Hells Angels, the Bandidos, Gremium MC and the Outlaws MC. It said these groups had worldwide contacts and were prepared to use violence to enforce club interests. The report counted four Gremium chapters in Bavaria, in Munich, Zwiesel and Hof, and noted that the Outlaws MC had formed in 2001 from various groups.

The federal criminal police office gave numbers in its organised-crime overview for 2010. Of 35 proceedings against motorcycle groups that year, up from 21 in 2009, 15 in 2008, nine in 2007 and two in 2006, three were against Gremium. For comparison it listed 20 against the Hells Angels, nine against the Bandidos and one against the Outlaws. In those 35 proceedings the main fields of activity were violent crime, including extortion and offences against life, and drug trafficking; the passage saved does not break these down by club. Suspicion is not proof, and the 2010 figures count investigations, not convictions.

On 3 July 2013, the federal interior minister, Hans-Peter Friedrich, banned the "Regionalverband Gremium Motorcycle Club (MC) Sachsen". According to tagesschau.de, a large police operation searched homes and clubhouses in Berlin, Brandenburg, Lower Saxony, Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt that morning. The ministry said the group posed a "serious danger to individual legal interests and the public", and that its structures and activities were geared towards violent expansion of territory and power, chiefly in Saxony and Brandenburg. It also accused the group of the attempted killing of a teenager on 31 December 2011 in Brandenburg. The Berliner Zeitung wrote that about 650 officers rang at some 60 doors in Berlin and Brandenburg at 6 a.m., among them special-forces units and the federal police's GSG 9, and that evidence was seized. It reported that this was the first time a whole regional association of motorcycle clubs had been dissolved.

The chapters named in the ban were Gremium MC Dresden, Chemnitz and Plauen, Nomads Eastside and Härte Plauen, according to the newspaper. The same day Brandenburg's interior minister, Dietmar Woidke, banned two Hells Angels groups there. The Berliner Zeitung traced the escalation between the Hells Angels and Gremium to an attempted murder on 25 December 2011 in Königs Wusterhausen: a Gremium member was attacked after an alleged insult to the Hells Angels' president. As a consequence, the paper wrote, an uninvolved 16-year-old was stabbed in the same town around New Year's Eve by rockers from Saxony, Brandenburg and Berlin; both victims survived, and the newspaper said both cases were before courts in Cottbus and Potsdam. It also reported that the Gremium leader, 40, had reportedly been arrested in the raids. The Berlin club had 34 members according to police, and experts did not rule out that members would now move to Gremium chapters in Berlin and Brandenburg. The club, the newspaper said, was surprised by the raid and wanted to reorganise. Tagesschau noted that rockers generally deny involvement in crime.

Four years later, on 14 September 2017, the club said it had filed a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court against a change to the associations law that parliament passed in January 2017 and which took effect in March 2017. It said the change violated its rights to freedom of association and expression, and called the widened ban on club symbols a kind of "guilt by association".

Danish papers watched the club's approach to their country in 2014. B.T. reported on 27 June that Gremium was working to open a chapter in Denmark, citing sources in the gang scene. Michael Ask, head of the police's national intelligence centre, confirmed that the police had heard so and that talks had reportedly been held in Germany between the club and people from the Danish gang scene. B.T.'s sources said the would-be founders were hardened violent offenders with immigrant backgrounds who had earlier been linked to the Nørrebro scene. The paper said German police regard Gremium as a collection of criminals on a par with the Hells Angels and Bandidos, that it is friendly with the Satudarah club and a competitor of the other two, and that there had been bloody clashes. It also reported an unconfirmed rumour of a Norwegian patch-over.

In September 2014 Ekstra Bladet described a new Danish splinter group, called Black 7, linked to Gremium's Berlin chapter. It had, according to the paper's information, about seven members, no clubhouse and no motorcycles yet. Asked directly, people said to belong to it denied any knowledge. Ask declined to comment on individual groups. The paper added that a Norwegian outlet had written in July that Gremium had set up four chapters in Norway under the same name.

By 21 October 2016, Netavisen Sjælland reported, Gremium had held a prospect chapter in Denmark since the start of 2015. At its opening party on 7 February that year the police of South Zealand and Lolland-Falster imposed a stop-and-search zone because of tension in the town between the group and the Bandidos. The group had also been in conflict with a group called Brothas, now part of Black Jackets, and shootings between the two followed. In September 2016 the prospects exchanged their "P/G MC" patches for full "Gremium MC Denmark" ones; the chapter's name remained Copenhagen Central.

The club itself rejects the portrait drawn by officials. Its website says, "contrary to claims spread for media effect by German politics, in particular some interior ministers and parts of the media", that Gremium is a traditional German motorcycle club in which riding together and friendship come first, and that it accepts and respects German law. It also says that "when one of them does evil, we condemn them all, but when they do good, we deny it" is the way the press and interior ministries treat bikers. The authorities see it differently: the Bavarian report said organised-crime-type behaviour had repeatedly been found among members of such groups, and in 2013 a regional association was banned. The Karlsruhe trial, in which even the prosecutor no longer mentioned the criminal-association charge in his closing speech and 16 members were convicted as individuals, remains the one large court test described in the pages used here.
